claims.text: A relative path is measured from the working directory of the process that asks, not from the folder holding the compiled program and not from the folder holding the source file.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: Path.GetFullPath(String) Remarks ('uses the current directory and current volume information to fully qualify path') and Environment.CurrentDirectory

claims.text: A process starts with the working directory whoever launched it hands over; a terminal hands over the folder it is sitting in, so the folder you type the command in decides what a relative path means at start-up.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API: Directory.GetCurrentDirectory Remarks (distinct from the directory the process was started from); Bash Reference Manual, 'Command Execution Environment'

claims.text: A path that names its own starting point — /tmp/demo/app.conf on Linux, C:\demo\app.conf on Windows — is absolute and means the same file whatever the working directory is; any other path is relative and is measured from the working directory.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/io/file-path-formats (fully qualified vs relative paths); Path.GetFullPath(String) Remarks and Examples

claims.text: When a bare name is opened in a folder the process may search, the two failures you will meet are: nothing is at the resolved path, or the user the process runs as may not open what is there. If the folder itself is closed to that user, the answer is 'not allowed' whether or not the file exists.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API: File.ReadAllText Exceptions table (FileNotFoundException vs UnauthorizedAccessException); learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/io/handling-io-errors

claims.text: In .NET 10, Directory.GetCurrentDirectory() returns the current working directory of the running process.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: System.IO.Directory.GetCurrentDirectory

claims.text: In .NET 10, AppContext.BaseDirectory is the folder the program's own files were started from, and it is not necessarily the working directory of the process.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: System.AppContext.BaseDirectory ('the file path of the base directory of the application'); compare Directory.GetCurrentDirectory

claims.text: In .NET 10, Path.GetFullPath(string) turns a relative path into an absolute one using the current working directory, without checking whether anything exists there.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: System.IO.Path.GetFullPath(String), Remarks ('The file or directory specified by path is not required to exist')

claims.text: In .NET 10, File.ReadAllText throws FileNotFoundException when the folder exists but the file does not, DirectoryNotFoundException when a folder in the path does not exist, and UnauthorizedAccessException when the caller is not permitted to open what is there.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: System.IO.File.ReadAllText(String), Exceptions table

claims.text: In .NET 10, FileNotFoundException.FileName holds the path that was tried, which is why the sample can print the path the program actually looked at.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: System.IO.FileNotFoundException.FileName ('Gets the name of the file that cannot be found')

claims.text: At stage-0, the read-config-file sample resolves app.conf at the top of the repository when run from there, and inside samples/DonHang.Samples when run from there, from the same compiled files.
claims.source_hint: verified on the stage-0 tree (.NET SDK 10.0.300): the sample run from the repository root and from samples/DonHang.Samples prints a different third line, the same AppContext.BaseDirectory

claims.text: Every file records an owner, a group, and which of reading, writing and executing is allowed for the owner, for the group and for everyone else.
claims.source_hint: GNU coreutils manual, 'File permissions' (the three classes of user and the three permissions); stat(1) format sequence %A (whose first character is the file type, not a permission)

claims.text: stat -c '%A %U:%G %n' prints the permissions in symbolic form, the owner name, the group name and the file name of one file.
claims.source_hint: stat(1) manual, format sequences %A (access rights in human-readable form), %U (owner name), %G (group name), %n (file name); matches the captured stage-0 output

claims.text: At stage-0, scripts/computer/permissions.sh prints -rw-r--r-- for the file it has just created and -rw------- for the same file after chmod 600.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/permissions.txt lines 2-3, captured by the example repository's CI; the 644 comes from the lab image's umask, not pinned (see open_questions)

claims.text: The permissions -rw------- let the file's owner read and write it and let no other ordinary user do anything with it; a process running as root is not stopped by these bits when it reads or writes a file.
claims.source_hint: GNU coreutils 'Symbolic modes' / chmod(1); path_resolution(7) on the root exemption; in the stage-0 lab box a mode 000 file owned by another uid is read by root and refused to nobody

claims.text: At stage-0 the script runs as root, and the operating system does not apply these permission bits to root, so the file is still read after chmod 600 removes every other user's access.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/permissions.txt line 1 (whoami: root), lines 2-3 (root:root) and line 11 (the final cat succeeds); path_resolution(7) on the root exemption

claims.text: At stage-0, the same command `cat app.conf` prints the file while the working directory is /tmp/demo and reports no such file while it is /, and the absolute path /tmp/demo/app.conf works from both.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/permissions.txt lines 5-11, produced by scripts/computer/permissions.sh lines 17-26

claims.text: A text file written by a Windows tool that follows the Windows convention ends each line with one byte more than a Linux tool writes, and a plain copy carries those bytes across unchanged.
claims.source_hint: git-scm.com/docs/gitattributes, the `text` and `eol` attributes ('the default is eol=crlf on Windows and eol=lf on all other platforms'); note that a Git checkout is not a plain copy and may convert

claims.text: A program on Linux reading a line that still carries the extra Windows byte treats that byte as part of the last word on the line, which is why a copied script fails naming a command that looks correctly spelled.
claims.source_hint: reproducible in the stage-0 lab box: printf '#!/bin/sh\r\npwd\r\n' > f.sh; bash f.sh reports $'pwd\r': command not found; git-scm.com/docs/gitattributes (why eol=lf is set for scripts)

claims.text: An editor and a program you run are separate processes that may run as different users and from different working directories, so the same bare file name can succeed in one and fail in the other.
claims.source_hint: follows from claims 1 and 4; verifiable by opening a file in an editor while a process running as another user is refused the same path

claims.text: A program that runs a script takes the first word of each command line as the name of the thing to run, so a byte another system leaves at the end of a line stays glued to the last word on that line — the command name itself when the line holds only one word.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Shell Operation' (a line is split into words; the first word is the command name looked up); reproducible with the one-word and two-word CRLF scripts of claim 18

claims.text: In .NET 10, `dotnet run` passes the arguments after `--` to the application being run rather than treating them as options of `dotnet run` itself.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-run, the `--` argument delimiter

claims.text: In .NET 10, `dotnet run` without `--project` runs the project found in the current directory, so the option can be left out when the working directory is the project's own folder.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-run, the `--project` option and its default

claims.text: In .NET 10, `dotnet run` builds the project before running it — it depends on `dotnet build` — unless it is told not to build.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-run, Description ('The command depends on the dotnet build command to build the code') and the --no-build option

claims.text: In the symbolic form stat prints for %A, the letters after the leading file-type character say what the owner may do and then what other users may do, using r for reading, w for writing, x for executing and - where that action is not allowed.
claims.source_hint: GNU coreutils manual, 'Mode Structure' and 'Symbolic modes'; stat(1) format sequence %A (access rights in human-readable form)
